_about: Drafted by Claude on 2026-11-24 (E3, prompt 74); approved by Nav on 2026-11-24 (prompt 75). Vesta's 30 fun facts for the Destination file card and /destinations/vesta, one a day, in the same format as mars.json. Every fact was checked on 2026-11-24 against the NASA page in 'source'; 'quote' is the supporting text from that page (' … ' joins two parts of the same page). None repeats a milestone fact (content/milestones/vesta.json).

facts.fact: Vesta is the second most massive body in the main asteroid belt, after the dwarf planet Ceres.
facts.quote: Vesta is the second most massive body in the main asteroid belt … Only dwarf planet Ceres is more massive in that region of rocky debris between Mars and Jupiter.

facts.fact: Vesta alone holds almost 9% of the total mass of the main asteroid belt.
facts.quote: Vesta is the second most massive body in the main asteroid belt, accounting for almost 9% of the total mass

facts.fact: Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers discovered Vesta at Bremen, in Germany, on 29 March 1807.
facts.quote: Vesta was discovered at Bremen, Germany, on Mar. 29, 1807 by Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers

facts.fact: Vesta was the fourth asteroid ever discovered.
facts.quote: Vesta was the fourth asteroid ever to be discovered.

facts.fact: Olbers let the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, who had worked out its orbit, name the new asteroid.
facts.quote: gave the honor of naming the new asteroid to German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, who had computed its orbit

facts.fact: Gauss named Vesta after the Roman goddess of the hearth and household.
facts.quote: Gauss named it Vesta after the goddess of the hearth and household in Roman mythology.

facts.fact: Olbers thought, wrongly, that Ceres and Pallas were pieces of a destroyed planet.
facts.quote: He proposed—incorrectly as it turned out—that Ceres and Pallas were fragments of a destroyed planet

facts.fact: Vesta is the largest asteroid, about 530 km across. (Ceres is bigger, but it counts as a dwarf planet.)
facts.quote: Vesta – the largest asteroid at about 329 miles (530 kilometers) in diameter

facts.fact: Vesta is almost round, so it is very nearly classed as a dwarf planet.
facts.quote: The giant asteroid is almost spherical, and so is nearly classified a dwarf planet.

facts.fact: Vesta's surface covers about twice the area of California.
facts.quote: About twice the area of California, Vesta is the second largest object in the asteroid belt after the dwarf planet Ceres.

facts.fact: Unlike most asteroids, Vesta has separated into a crust, a mantle and a core.
facts.quote: Unlike most known asteroids, Vesta has separated into crust, mantle and core

facts.fact: Dawn found that Vesta's gravity fits an iron core about 225 km (140 miles) across.
facts.quote: Dawn also found that Vesta's gravity field is consistent with the presence of an iron core around 140 miles in diameter

facts.fact: Vesta has one of the widest ranges of brightness seen on any rocky body in the Solar System.
facts.quote: Vesta has one of the largest brightness ranges observed on any rocky body in our solar system.

facts.fact: About 300 dark asteroids, 1 to 10 km wide, are thought to have hit Vesta in the last 3.5 billion years.
facts.quote: about 300 dark asteroids with diameters ranging from one to 10 km (0.6 to six miles) hit Vesta during the last 3.5 billion years

facts.fact: Vesta's Rheasilvia crater is about 500 km wide: some 95% of the asteroid's mean diameter.
facts.quote: the Rheasilvia crater, which is about 310 miles (500 kilometers) wide—some 95 percent of the asteroid's mean diameter.

facts.fact: Rheasilvia is about 19 km (12 miles) deep.
facts.quote: Rheasilvia’s width is 95% of the mean diameter of Vesta and it is about 12 miles deep

facts.fact: The peak in the middle of Rheasilvia rises 19 to 26 km (12 to 16 miles), and it's more than 160 km wide.
facts.quote: Its central peak rises 12-16 miles and is more than 100 miles wide

facts.fact: Rheasilvia's central peak could rival Olympus Mons on Mars as the biggest mountain in the Solar System.
facts.quote: making it compete with Mars' Olympus Mons as the largest mountain the in solar system

facts.fact: Another huge crater on Vesta, Veneneia, is about 400 km wide.
facts.quote: Another huge crater is Veneneia, which is about 250 miles (400 km) in diameter.

facts.fact: A system of troughs runs right round Vesta's equator.
facts.quote: An extensive system of troughs encircles Vesta's equatorial region.

facts.fact: The biggest of Vesta's troughs, Divalia Fossa, is bigger than the Grand Canyon.
facts.quote: The largest, named Divalia Fossa, is bigger than the Grand Canyon.

facts.fact: The two giant impacts in Vesta's southern hemisphere also made the troughs that circle it.
facts.quote: the two giant impacts caused planet-encircling trough systems to form

facts.fact: Vesta is thought to have lost about 1% of its mass in a giant collision less than a billion years ago.
facts.quote: Vesta is believed to have lost about one percent of its mass less than a billion years ago

facts.fact: The Vesta family of asteroids is probably debris from that collision.
facts.quote: The Vesta family of asteroids is probably debris from this collision.

facts.fact: Scientists think about 6% of all the meteorites found on Earth came from that ancient impact on Vesta.
facts.quote: Scientist believe that about 6 percent of all meteorites we find on Earth are a result of this ancient impact in deep space.

facts.fact: Dawn confirmed that Vesta is where the HED meteorites (howardites, eucrites and diogenites) found on Earth come from.
facts.quote: The Dawn mission confirmed that Vesta is the parent body of the howardite-eucrite-diogenite (HED) meteorites

facts.fact: Dawn found gullies in some young craters on Vesta, which scientists read as signs that water flowed there for a short time.
facts.quote: pitted terrains and gullies were found in several young craters … interpreted as evidence of volatile releases and transient water flow

facts.fact: Thanks to its ion engines, Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different bodies in the Solar System: Vesta, then Ceres.
facts.quote: allows Dawn to go into orbit around two different solar system bodies, a first for any spacecraft

facts.fact: Even the Hubble Space Telescope could see the scar of Vesta's giant impacts, with a peak in its centre.
facts.quote: was apparent even in Hubble Space Telescope images, which also discerned a peak in the center

facts.fact: NASA calls Dawn, which visited Vesta, its first truly interplanetary spaceship.
facts.quote: Dawn was NASA’s first truly interplanetary spaceship.
